question:
Patient note:
A 59-year-old man was brought to the urgent access clinic by his spouse late this morning because the lower half of his right leg had become clearly larger and tight over the prior twenty-four hours after nearly a full week spent mostly in bed recovering from a febrile influenza-A infection that had left him too exhausted to do more than shuffle to the bathroom and back; he estimates he remained supine at least twenty-two hours per day from last Saturday through Wednesday evening before beginning to feel stronger yesterday. Earlier today, while dressing to leave the house for the first time since the illness began, he noticed his right pant leg clung snugly around the calf and that pulling on a walking shoe required more effort than on the left side. He reports no fall, twist, kick, or new exercise routine, denies insect bites, animal scratches, rashes, or local trauma, and has not traveled farther than the living-room sofa in ten days. He denies chest pain, pleuritic discomfort, dyspnea beyond a mild residual dry cough, hemoptysis, palpitations, syncope, fevers since Monday, chills, night sweats, abdominal pain, flank discomfort, dysuria, or recent weight change. He has never experienced a clot in the legs or lungs, never been told he carries a thrombophilia, and no first-degree relative has venous thromboembolism. His medical history includes well-controlled type 2 diabetes managed with metformin 1000 mg twice daily, hyperlipidemia on atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and allergic rhinitis treated seasonally with intranasal fluticasone; there is no chronic heart, liver, or kidney disease. He underwent an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy nine years ago and a screening colonoscopy four years back, but has had no operations, invasive procedures, casts, splints, braces, or limb weakness in the past year. He does not take hormone replacement, corticosteroids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or anticoagulants, stopped smoking twelve years ago after a 15-pack-year exposure, drinks two glasses of wine weekly, and denies illicit drug use. On arrival—before any medication or intravenous fluids were administered—he sat upright but kept the right knee extended on a pillow for comfort. Triage vitals read temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 130/78 mm Hg, heart rate 92 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air. Cardiac examination revealed a crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lung fields were clear to auscultation with only faint end-expiratory pops at the right base consistent with resolving viral pneumonia. The abdomen was soft, nontender, and nondistended with no hepatosplenomegaly. Inspection of the lower extremities demonstrated a distinct bulge over the posteromedial aspect of the right calf accompanied by a lattice of dilated, straight, non-tortuous superficial veins functioning as collateral channels coursing from the mid-gastrocnemius toward the popliteal fossa, changes absent on the contralateral limb; skin temperature felt equal bilaterally and coloration remained normal pink with no erythema, hyperpigmentation, or stasis dermatitis. A flexible tape measure placed exactly 10 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity recorded a circumference of 42.0 cm on the symptomatic side versus 38.4 cm on the left, a difference of 3.6 cm; at mid-thigh the limbs were nearly identical at 54 cm, supporting localization of swelling to the calf rather than the entire leg. Thumb pressure maintained for five seconds over the anterior tibial crest produced immediate recoil without an indentation, mirroring the response on the left and indicating absence of pitting. Careful palpation along the femoral triangle, adductor canal, and popliteal fossa revealed no discrete tenderness or palpable cord; gastrocnemius and soleus bellies were supple, and passive ankle dorsiflexion elicited only a sense of tightness rather than sharp pain. Hip, knee, and ankle moved through full active and passive ranges without crepitus or effusion. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were 2+ and symmetric, capillary refill of the toes was under two seconds, and monofilament testing showed intact light-touch sensibility. No inguinal or popliteal lymphadenopathy was detected, Achilles tendon was intact, and there was no posterior knee fullness to suggest a ruptured Baker cyst. Point-of-care labs obtained before any anticoagulant exposure revealed hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, leukocyte count 6.9 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 268 × 10⁹/L, serum creatinine 0.94 mg/dL, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 19 U/L, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 seconds. A resting 12-lead ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 90 beats/min without ST-T abnormalities. Portable anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the tibia and fibula ordered by his primary care physician earlier this morning showed intact bony structures and only soft-tissue prominence. No cellulitic erythema, myofascial herniation, tendinous rupture, lymphedema, or compartment syndrome signs were evident to account for the asymmetric calf enlargement. Given the objectively measured difference exceeding three centimeters, the visibly engorged superficial venous channels on the affected side, the recent five-day period of near-continuous recumbency, the lack of prior thrombotic episodes, absence of neurologic weakness or orthopedic immobilization, and the scarcity of any alternative musculoskeletal or infectious explanation on examination, a comprehensive duplex ultrasound of the right lower-extremity deep venous system has been ordered on an urgent basis while the patient remains under observation in the evaluation bay.

Question: What is the patient's score of Wells' criteria for Deep Vein Thrombosis? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Wells DVT score assigns 1 point per positive criterion and subtracts 2 if an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely as DVT. At presentation:
- Bedridden for at least 3 days or recent major surgery: nearly continuously in bed for 5 days, +1.
- Calf at least 3 cm larger than the other side: 42.0 − 38.4 = 3.6 cm at 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity, +1.
- Collateral superficial veins (nonvaricose): visible on the right calf, +1.
- Active cancer, paralysis/paresis or recent cast immobilization, localized deep venous tenderness, entire-leg swelling, unilateral pitting edema, and previous DVT: none documented, 0 each.
- Alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT: none identified, 0 rather than −2.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 3.
Final answer: 3
